[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 2]
2. Another source of uncertainty and one that is fully acknowledged in the study is the
issue of fixed rooting depths prescribed in the ESMs. Even if the rooting depths show
inter-pft variability, there is large variance intra-pft and this would cause a lot of
spatial variability in soil water uptake. I acknowledge that this is not something that
can be easily addressed but should, ideally be discussed. For example, In line 337, the
authors say that ET is enhanced but with shallower root depths, the vegetation might
not have the capacity to access potentially depleted soil moisture.
[Response] Thank you for raising the criticism of Earth System Models (ESMs)
regarding their fixed rooting depths for specific plant functional types (PFTs), which,
we agree, is a key source of uncertainty in eco-hydrological modeling. The rooting
depth is known to vary considerably across gradients of hydroclimate, soil properties,
and topography7–9. For example, plants typically develop deeper roots in arid regions
8,9—a strategic adaptation to access deeper soil moisture, which contrasts with their
investment in aboveground growth in water-abundant areas10. In our model-based
global forestation experiment, the fixed rooting depth cannot capture the growth
dynamic of roots, and thus may overestimate the actual root depth of newly
established trees. This bias may propagate to an overestimation of the forestation-
induced increase in evapotranspiration (ET) and the associated soil drying,
particularly in wet regions such as Southeast Asia. In the revised manuscript, we have
included a few sentences in Discussion to highlight the limitation of fix root depth,
as detailed below:
“Second, our simulations do not account for the spatial and temporal dynamics of tree
rooting depths, which are prescribed as fixed values for each plant functional type
(PFT) in land surface models. Hence, the models do not represent how rooting depths
vary with hydroclimates, soil properties, topography, and forest age94–96. This
simplification may lead to biases, since observations show that the rooting depth tend
to increase with aridity to access deeper water sources95,96, and evolve over a tree’s
lifetime97. For instance, in humid regions like Southeast Asia, using a fixed,
potentially overestimated rooting depth for newly planted trees could overestimate the
projected increase in ET and the consequent soil water depletion (Fig. 1).” (Lines
518-526)
[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 3]
3. This is not exactly a suggestion but more of an observation: it is interesting that the
runoff increases in the tropics and decreases in the boreal regions. As the boreal
regions are fairly humid, it would be interesting to see if they go past a key
aridity threshold (humid to dry-subhumid for example).
[Response] Thank you for sharing this insightful perspective. To test whether
forestation-reduced runoff in boreal regions would shift the regional aridity state, we
link the hydrological responses directly to aridity conditions using the Aridity Index
(AI, the ratio of precipitation [P] to potential evapotranspiration [PET]) (Fig. R4).
Following the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) classification, an AI
(P/PET) greater than 0.65 denotes humid conditions, and an AI between 0.5 and 0.65
indicates dry sub-humid conditions.
Our results indicate that boreal regions in Eurasia remain to be classified as a humid
region (AI > 0.65) following large-scale forestation, with the spatial distribution of the
humid and dry sub-humid areas being almost unchanged. This suggests that while
forestation does reduce runoff in boreal regions, it does not trigger a shift in the
region’s climatic state from humid to dry sub-humid.
Fig. R4 Spatial patterns of dryness conditions in CTL (a) and SCE (Bastin_Full
scenario, b). Colors represent regions of different aridity levels classified using an
aridity index according to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 4]
4. Much of the results and the consequent conclusions depend on how good the
hydrological model within ORCHIDEE is? Considering that LSMs are not intended
for hydrological modelling, the authors should provide more details on how the
runoff from the model is validated, and to what degree can they be trusted? In this regard the
manuscript is very light on the details.
[Response] We sincerely thank you for this comment which motivated us to evaluate
the mode performance in simulating runoff. In light of your comment, we conducted a
validation of the simulated runoff against observed streamflow data derived from the
Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive (GSIM)11,12. In the Supplementary
Text 3, we provide details on this streamflow database and describe the data screening
criteria and processing, as also copied here:
“We conducted a validation of the simulated runoff using streamflow observations
from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive (GSIM)1,2, which provides
daily records of streamflow from over 30,000 stations worldwide. To ensure
comparability with model’s coarse spatial resolution and its lack of representation of
direct human interventions (e.g., dam construction, irrigation), we screened the
available catchments based the following criteria: (1) with a drainage area greater
than 20,000 km2; (2) with at least 15 years of complete annual streamflow records
between 1971 and 2010; (3) with ‘high’ or ‘medium’ boundary quality, indicating less
than 10% difference between the calculated and reported drainage area; (4) with
irrigation areas < 1% of total area or reservoir capacity < 10% of mean annual
streamflow; (5) Only catchments for which four homogeneity tests (i.e., the standard
normal homogeneity test3, the Buishand range test4, the Pettitt test5, and the von
Neumann ratio test6, adopted by the GSIM data) all fail to reject the null hypothesis of
no break-point in the time series at the 1% significance level were selected. The
catchmental irrigation area and reservoir capacity, and quality control for catchment
boundaries, are all derived from the GSIM metadata.
Applying these criteria led to a total of 270 catchments. The locations of these
catchments and the number of valid annual observations are shown in the
Supplementary Fig. 26a. For comparability with models’ runoff output, mean annual
runoff (in mm day-1) from observations were obtained by dividing the river discharge
(m3 day-1) by the station’s upstream catchment area (km2). For the simulated runoff by
IPSL and CESM (based on the CTL run), we first interpolated model output to a 1°
resolution. For each selected catchment, the catchment-scale runoff was calculated as
the areal-weighted average of grid cells falling within the catchment.”
(Supplementary Text 3).
Fig. R5 (also appears as Supplementary Fig. 26 in the revised version) Supplementary
Fig. 26 Evaluation of the model-simulated mean annual runoff across the 270
catchments. (a) Spatial distribution of the 270 selected catchments and the number of
years with available observations per catchment. (b, c) Scatter plots of annual mean
runoff simulated by IPSL (b) and CESM (c) versus corresponding observations across
the 270 catchments. The size of the markers represents the catchment area, and the color
of the markers denotes the number of available observation years for each catchment.
(d) Box plots of the difference between modelled and observed annual mean runoff,
showing the median (horizontal lines), 25th, 75th quartiles, maximum and minimum
values (top and bottom of the whiskers), outliers (dots) and the 95% confidence interval
for the median (notches).
Using streamflow observations from the 270 selected catchments (as shown in Fig.
R5a), we evaluated the performance of modelled runoff. As expected, IPSL-
simulated runoff exhibits notable deviations from observed values especially in large
catchments (Fig. R5b). This is because IPSL does not account for the effects of
urbanization, anthropogenic land-use changes, and river routing processes within the
catchments particularly those large ones. Despite this difference for specific
catchments, we find an overall significant positive correlation (r = 0.66, p < 0.01)
between the IPSL simulations and observations (Fig. 5b), indicating that IPSL
successfully captures characteristics of runoff in ‘wet’ versus ‘dry’ catchments.
Importantly, across all available catchments, the median difference between IPSL
estimates and observations is significantly indistinguishable from zero (Fig. 5d),
suggesting no systemic bias in IPSL simulations of runoff at the continental scale.
Furthermore, we find that IPSL outperforms CESM in runoff simulations. Evaluation
of CESM-based estimates show a weak, though significant, correlation (r) of 0.20 (p
< 0.01) (Fig. R5c), and a significant negative deviation of the modelled runoff from
observations, indicating a systemic underestimation of runoff (Fig. R5d). Given this
apparent discrepancy, we chose not to present the CESM-based estimates in the main
figures, but instead include this as an additional model test to verify our primary
findings based on IPSL. In the revised manuscript, we presented the evaluation of
model performance based on streamflow observations. The added text reads as
follows:
“Model performance was further evaluated using observed streamflow records of 270
screened catchments from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive
(GSIM)109,110 (Supplementary Text 3). The IPSL-CM successfully reproduces cross-
catchment runoff variability (r = 0.66, p < 0.01), with the median of model-
observation difference statistically indistinguishable from zero. This indicates no
systematic bias in the IPSL-modelled runoff, supporting the model capability for
assessing afforestation-induced runoff responses (Supplementary Fig. 26).” (Lines
558-564 in revised manuscript);
“It is worth noting that while CESM-simulated runoff is significantly correlated with
observations, CESM overall underperforms IPSL (Supplementary Fig. 26). We
therefore present the CESM-based results in the Supplementary Information to
support the robustness of our primary findings from IPSL.” (Lines 621-625 in revised
manuscript).
[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 5]
5. One of the biggest advantages of the study is the fully coupled model which
simulates the remote effects of local forestation, and which is very nicely shown in
the study. However, the authors predominantly focus on moisture recycling.
How about the impact of forestation on albedo changes and potential subsequent changes in
the atmospheric circulation? Does the increased atmospheric moisture affect the
stability of the atmosphere, thus affecting precipitation? In this regard, I find the
discussion of the results very sparse and superficial.
[Response] Thank you very much for recognizing the strength of our model approach
in capturing the remote effects of forestation, and for your suggestion of discussing
how afforestation influences precipitation by modifying atmospheric circulation. We
acknowledge that our original MS only addressed the influence of atmospheric
dynamics on precipitation through moisture budget decomposition, and the energy
balance perspective could help further understand the drivers.
First, we explored the influence of forestation-altered surface energy balance
(particularly reduced albedo, as shown in Fig. R6a) on atmospheric circulation
patterns. It should be noted that forestation alters surface energy balance by
modifying several key land surface characteristics, including albedo,
evapotranspiration and surface roughness. The combined changes in these
biogeophysical factors result in localized diabatic heating or cooling of the lower
atmosphere13. This modification in the thermal structure of the atmosphere further
initiates a stationary Rossby wave train (Fig. R6b), ultimately leading to the large-
scale circulation reorganization as documented in our original MS (Fig. R7).
For example, a large anticyclonic anomaly forms over Eurasia (Fig. R7c), which
weakens the prevailing westerlies and thus suppresses the advection of moisture from
the North Atlantic, consequently inhibiting advective precipitation (Fig. R8b).
Conversely, the southeasterly winds over Southeast China are strengthened, enhancing
moisture transport from the ocean and consequently favoring advective rainfall in that
region (Fig. R7c and R8b). In the revised version, we have expanded the discussion of
this energy balance aspect, as detailed below:
“The alteration in large-scale atmospheric circulation may be associated with
forestation-induced changes in surface energy balance, mainly through reduced
albedo44,51, which modify the thermal structure of the lower atmosphere and further
initiates a stationary Rossby wave train (Supplementary Fig. 25).” (Lines 497-500);
“For example, the southeasterly winds over Southeast China are strengthened,
enhancing moisture transport from the ocean and consequently favoring advective
rainfall in that region (Supplementary Figs. 14b and 15c).” (Lines 314-317);
“In addition, the large anticyclonic anomaly induced by forestation over Eurasia
weakens the prevailing westerlies, thereby reducing moisture advection from the
North Atlantic and inhibiting advective precipitation. (Supplementary Figs. 14b and
15c).” (Lines 333-336).
Second, we examined how forestation affects precipitation by changing atmospheric
stability. Actually, our previous manuscript has implicitly mentioned this mechanism.
In our moisture budget decomposition, we noted that afforestation-induced increased
atmospheric moisture raises the vertical moisture gradient (Fig. R7b), which enhances
upward moisture transport and facilitates the development of convective precipitation
(Fig. R7c and Fig. R8c). This strengthening upward motion indirectly corresponds to
a reduction in atmospheric stability. In the revised manuscript, we have additionally
employed the Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) metric to provide a
more direct and intuitive assessment of the changes in vertical stability and the
potential for convective development. Our new results demonstrate that the enhanced
near-surface moisture significantly increases CAPE by altering the vertical profile of
atmospheric moist static energy, thus providing more energy for vigorous convective
updrafts (Fig. R7a). In the revised manuscript, we have further elaborated on how
afforestation influences convective precipitation by changing atmospheric stability.
The added text reads as follows:
“This is because forestation significantly enhances the Convective Available Potential
Energy (CAPE) and the vertical gradient of specific humidity (Supplementary Fig.
15a, b), indicative of reduced atmospheric stability, thereby promoting the upward
motion of moisture (Supplementary Fig. 15c) and increasing convective precipitation
(Supplementary Fig. 14c).” (Lines 306-310)
Fig. R6 (also appears as Supplementary Fig. 25 in the revised version) Global
forestation-induced changes in surface albedo (a) and atmospheric circulation patterns
(b). In b, the shading and vectors indicate forestation-induced changes in 500 hPa
geopotential height and Plumb flux, respectively.
Fig R7 (also appears as Supplementary Fig. 15 in the revised version) Spatial patterns
of global forestation-induced changes in atmospheric processes. (a) Changes in

(vectors, unit: m s-1). These two variables are obtained by vertically integrating the
vertical velocity and wind at each level, respectively, using specific humidity as the
weighting factor. Black stipples in a and b denote statistically significant change at the
5% significance level using the paired sample t-test.
Fig. R8 (also appears as Supplementary Fig. 14 in the revised version) Moisture

[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 6]
6.Calling the Budyko parameter as “water retention capacity” is not exactly correct.
The partitioning of precipitation into evaporation is not only because more water is
stored in the watershed but also due to lateral flow out of the watershed. The
parameter is more an integral of all the factors that could not be explained by the
original non-parametric Budyko hypothesis. Maybe a better phrase is “partitioning
factor”?
[Response] We are grateful for this thoughtful comment on our interpretation of the
Budyko parameter n. We agree that, in the Budyko framework, n is a highly
sophisticated parameter that has integrated effects of many land surface processes14,15.
Respectfully, we contend that referring to the shape parameter n as a “partitioning
factor” is somehow misleading, as n was originally introduced to represent the
catchment’s physical properties beyond climate forcing16,17. Specifically, the
partitioning of precipitation into evapotranspiration (i.e., ET/PET) is jointly controlled
by climatic conditions (precipitation, PET) and n, as expressed by the Budyko
equation (Equation 1). Hence, the terminology “partitioning factor” may cause
confusion about n and ET/PET. This is also the reason for the rare use of this
terminology in the existing Budyko-related literature.

Actually, the interpretation of the shape parameter n as “water retention capacity” is
well-justified and widely adopted in the eco-hydrology literature14,15,18–20. Of course,
we acknowledge that most eco-hydrological studies, including those cited, do not
explicitly account for lateral flows between adjacent catchments. Furthermore, there is
little evidence to confirm whether accounting for such lateral water movement would
significantly alter Budyko-based hydrological assessments. Therefore, and to
incorporate your perspective, and to reflect the comprehensive nature of this shape
parameter, we chose to use a more general interpretation of n, referring to it as the
“surface parameter representing catchment characteristics”. In the revised manuscript,
we have explicitly clarified the meaning of this parameter and its connection of the
watershed’s water retention capacity. The amended texts are:
“This more universal negative effect of ∆𝑅 in mid-to-low latitudes arises from the
𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑑
forestation-induced increase in the surface parameter n (Supplementary Fig. 13b, d),
represents catchment characteristics governing runoff generation, and primarily
reflect the water retention capacity of the catchment26,60,75–77. The consistent increase
in n indicates that afforestation-induced catchmental changes overall enhances
rainfall portioning into regional ET, thereby reducing runoff.” (Lines 368-373)
[Reviewer #1 Major Comment 7]
7. In line with the previous comment, I feel that the utility of the Budyko hypothesis
has been stretched in the study. First, it was not originally intended to be used at grid-
cell level but more at large catchment-scale, and at very long-term timescales (greater
than 20–30 years). While a lot of studies have over-used the framework, I am not
exactly sure how to suggest improvements here but at the very least, these limitations
have to be acknowledged. For example, line 215: The applicability of the hypothesis
in cold regions is questionable.
[Response] Thank you for sharing your perspectives about the Budyko hypothesis.
Yes, applying the Budyko framework to grid-scale analysis is an extension of its
original intent. The rationale behind is, in the land surface model, runoff generation is
computed independently for each grid cell as a partitioning of rainfall, without
representation of lateral flow between cells21–23. In this context, each grid cell
functions as a small, hydrologically independent unit, therefore the Budyko theories
established and validated at the catchmental scale are also appliable to model’s grid
cells. This grid-cell application is extensive in the literature for separating the effects
of climate or land surface changes on surface runoff at regional to global scales24–26.
With respect to the requirement for long-term timescales, as you mention, we agree
that our previous 30-year analysis period might not be sufficiently long. In light of
your comment, we have extended the period of analysis to a longer 60-year timescale.
This extended 60-year period not only satisfies the steady-state assumption of the
Budyko framework, but also reduces the influence of inter-decadal or multi-decadal
climate variability on our attribution. The updated results based on the last 60 years
are consistent with the previous findings: the atmosphere-forest feedback dominates
the latitudinal divergence of the forestation-induced runoff response (please refer to
the updated main figures in the revised manuscript).
With respect to your concern about the applicability in cold regions, we agree that the
attribution using the Budyko framework might be biased over there. In these regions,
a considerable portion of precipitation falls as snow during winter, and subsequent
snowmelt in spring and early summer substantially contributes to seasonal runoff
generation. Critically, the effects of such snow-related processes, or more generally
precipitation characteristics (as see Reviewer #2’s Major Comment 9), are not
explicitly represented in the traditional Budyko framework. Specifically, in the
Budyko framework, the effects of precipitation characteristics (including snow-related
processes) on runoff were implicitly incorporated into the parameter n27, biasing our
interpretation of n changes as resulting from land surface processes. This provides the
rationale for the limited applicability in cold regions, as you point out.
To address potential bias related to precipitation characteristics, we separated
precipitation and runoff changes due to altered precipitation characteristics and
incorporated these into effects of atmospheric changes, following the approach
proposed by Zhou et al.25. We further decomposed the effects of the atmospheric
feedbacks (due to altered mean precipitation, PET, and precipitation characteristics),
and land surface changes (only due to catchment properties) on runoff under the
modified Budyko framework. In particular, this modification ensures applicability in
cold regions because snow-related biases have been corrected. The results based on
this extended method are consistent with our main conclusions, showing that forest-
atmosphere feedbacks primarily drive the latitudinal contrast in afforestation-induced
runoff changes, with decreases at high latitudes and increases in the tropics (Fig. R9).

[Reviewer #2 General Comment]
The manuscript by Fei Kan et al. addresses an important and timely topic: how global
forestation influences runoff, with a particular focus on latitudinal divergence driven
by forest-climate feedbacks. Using coupled land-atmosphere models and the Budyko
framework, the authors find that forestation leads to increased runoff in tropical
regions but reduced runoff in boreal regions. These findings underscore the
importance of incorporating hydrological considerations into afforestation strategies
aimed at climate mitigation. The manuscript is well-written and the technical details
are carefully presented. However, I have several concerns regarding model
uncertainty and methodological robustness that should be addressed before the
manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications.
[Response] We sincerely thank you for recognizing the timeliness of importance of
the topic and the perspective it adds to the existing literature. We also appreciate your
insightful comments on the model dependency and methodological robustness that
have guided us to strengthen our analyses and improve our MS. Below, we provide
details on how we tackled the issues raised and how these have contributed to the
refinement of our MS. We believe that these revisions have greatly improved the
quality of the MS.
[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 1]
This study bears strong resemblance to previous work on deforestation, particularly in
terms of methodology and key findings. While the authors conduct additional
analyses, the central conclusion—emphasizing the dominant role of forest-climate
feedbacks and regional divergence—is not entirely novel. Beyond these points, are
there any additional innovative insights that distinguish this study from prior
literature?
Ma, S., Zhou, S., Yu, B. & Song, J. Deforestation-induced runoff changes dominated
by forest-climate feedbacks. Science Advances 10, eadp3964 (2024)
[Response] We are grateful for this insightful comment and for highlighting the
connection to Ma et al.26 paper focused on deforestation. We are pleased to see this,
because it underscores the significance of understanding the forest-runoff relationship.
We acknowledge that the two studies share a methodological foundation in
quantifying forest-climate feedbacks, and both find their critical role in shaping the
spatial structure of runoff responses to forest cover change. However, we believe this
new work advances current understanding of this topic, and are conceptually distinct,
mechanistically richer, and directly relevant to future afforestation and climate–water
policy.
1. A different and more policy-relevant scientific question
While both studies focused on hydrological effects of forest change, the obvious
difference is that, Ma et al. focused on historical deforestation, whereas ours focus on
future potential afforestation. Compared to the land use history (often localized to
deforested areas, our work tackles a forward-looking and policy-critical question
central to global carbon neutrality and nature-based climate solutions. In particular, A
central consideration in forestation policies is determining the optimal locations for
tree planting to maximize climate benefits, our study provides a direct and concrete
answer to this from the perspective of hydrological outcomes. Our study highlights
that, while high-latitude afforestation has been questioned mainly for its albedo-
induced warming, our results add a hydrological caution, showing that such
afforestation could also exacerbate regional water scarcity (detailed in Lines 453-
465).
Furthermore, the effects of are not simply mirror images: the hydrological responses
to deforestation and afforestation can be highly nonlinear and spatially asymmetric,
owing to differences in baseline climate, land-atmosphere coupling strength, and
vegetation–radiation feedbacks. Importantly, regions identified as having potential
for afforestation are largely distinct from areas historically deforested — for
example, cropland or urban areas converted from forests are often unsuitable for
reverting back to forests — meaning that their hydrological impacts have remained
poorly constrained. In the revised manuscript, we further introduced three
progressively constrained forestation scenarios (detailed in Response to your
Comment 2), representing theoretical “maximum potential” to practically achievable
forestation under current climate limits. This provides actionable insight for policy
decisions of climate mitigation and water resource management in large-scale
afforestation planning, an aspect absent from previous deforestation-focused analyses.
We have highlighted the importance of investigating the hydrological impacts of
potential afforestation in the revised Introduction, written as: “Most existing
modelling studies focus on the feedbacks of deforestation41,43,45,46. However, given that
the hydrological responses to afforestation and deforestation are asymmetric and that
the regions suitable for potential afforestation are largely distinct from historically
deforested areas44,47,48, it remains essential to investigate the hydrological
consequences of afforestation. In addition, these simulations predominantly rely on
idealized (e.g., 100% or 50%) or historical afforestation/deforestation
scenarios44,49,50. Such scenarios fail to account for current and local-specific climate
constraints on achievable forestation potential6,44,50, thus potentially limiting their
applicability in guiding science-based strategies for future afforestation initiatives.”
(Lines 85-94).
2. Novel interpretation of the regional divergence
Our study does not merely replicate regional patterns reported previously; it
establishes a mechanistic framework linking forestation-induced hydrological effects
to thermal (cold vs. warm) and dryness (wet vs. dry) gradients. We reveal that
atmospheric feedback effects follow the thermal gradients, whereas land surface
effects follow the dryness gradients. Specifically, atmospheric feedbacks dominate
runoff increases in warm, humid regions but suppress runoff in cold, high-latitude
regions—revealing a predictable latitudinal structure of forest–climate coupling.
Meanwhile, the land-surface (biophysical) effects show a unimodal relationship with
the dryness index (PET/P), with the strongest runoff suppression near the transitional
(energy–water co-limited) zone. These organizing patterns have not been reported in
prior studies and provide a unified theoretical basis for interpreting regional
hydrological consequences of forest expansion. We have also emphasized this point in
the Discussion section, written as: “In contrast to the thermally/latitudinally
dependent forest-atmosphere feedbacks, afforestation-induced land surface effect
drives spatially consistent runoff suppression along the dryness gradient, reaching
maximum intensity in transitional regions where the PET/P value approaches unity.”
(Lines 413-416).
3. Improved mechanistic understanding of the patterns
Beyond quantifying total runoff responses, our analysis offers a deeper mechanistic
understanding of the processes underlying the observed spatial divergence. For the
atmospheric feedback, we decomposed precipitation changes into thermodynamic
versus dynamic components of the moisture budget, and further partitioned PET
changes into energy and humidity-driven terms. These analyses reveal that enhanced
tropical precipitation primarily arises from strengthened large-scale circulation and
moisture convergence, whereas PET changes exhibit opposite latitudinal tendencies
governed by the balance between available energy and atmospheric moisture demand.
For the land-surface effects, our integration of the Budyko framework provides a first-
principles explanation for the nonlinear runoff response, showing why afforestation-
induced suppression peaks near the transitional PET/P ≈ 1 boundary. Together, these
process-level insights move beyond the diagnostic scope of prior deforestation
analyses, offering a unified, physically interpretable framework for future forest–
hydrology interactions under climate change. Associated discussion regarding this
point can be found in Lines 405-419.
[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 2]
The authors adopt a “full-potential forestation” scenario. Is this scenario similarly
idealized as those used in earlier studies? How realistic is it under current and future
climate and land-use constraints? Could comparable forestation pathways realistically
occur in future scenarios? A critical issue is the reliability and accuracy of the
simulated runoff responses. To what extent have these runoff outputs been validated
against observations? If observational constraints are limited, how confident can we
be in the attribution results derived from these model simulations?
[Response] Thank you for raising these thought-provoking questions about the “full-
potential forestation” scenario. Your questions and concerns primarily focus on two
key aspects: (1) the feasibility of our “full-potential forestation” scenario, and (2) the
reliability of simulated runoff from the climate models.
(1) Feasibility of the full-potential forestation scenario
The full-potential forestation (Bastin_Full) scenario used in this study represents the
theoretical maximum tree cover that current climatic conditions could support, as
defined in Bastin et al.1. Unlike previous studies that employed simplified “100%” or
“50%” afforestation scenarios, Bastin_Full represents the upper-bound afforestation
potential under current climate suitability. However, this scenario does not account for
other limiting factors such as land-use constraints, socio-economic feasibility, shifts in
future climate regimes, and land-climate feedbacks (e.g., albedo effects). As such,
afforestation to this full potential is unlikely to be realized in practice. Our goal in
using this idealized scenario is not to predict future land cover but to provide a
theoretical framework for assessing the potential hydrological effects of forestation
under a hypothetical upper-bound scenario.
To address this limitation and evaluate the robustness of our results, we additionally
designed two sensitivity scenarios: Bastin_Refined_Climate and
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land. Specifically, Bastin_Refined_Climate, is based upon
Bastin_Full but excludes areas with frequent fire and regions with additional climate
constraints due to forest-induced albedo changes. This scenario addresses two major
critiques of the Bastin’s data: the overestimation of tree cover potential in grassland
and savanna ecosystems with frequent fire, and the modeling of new tree cover in
water-limited regions where trees reduce albedo and induce net climate warming2–4.
Applying these constraints lead to a lower estimated afforestation potential,
particularly in tropical grassland and savanna ecosystems across Africa (Fig. R10b).
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land, is an extended version of Bastin_RefinedClimate that
additionally excludes croplands, built-up lands and wetlands. This represents the most
feasible forestation scenario. We excluded urban and agricultural areas due to their
critical importance for human sustenance and socio-economic activities. We applied
the wetland precautionary exclusions to protect large soil organic carbon (SOC) 
stocks that may be vulnerable to losses following the establishment of trees5,6.
Compared with the Bastin_Refined_Climate scenario, the further reduction in
afforestation area in Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land predominantly occurs in
cropland-dominated regions like Europe, African croplands, Southeast Asia, and
eastern South America (Fig. R10c). Specific details on the sensitivity scenario settings
and the exclusionary datasets used can be found in the updated Methods section,
written as:
“Two sensitivity experiments with constrained forestation
As previously noted, the Bastin et al.’s data likely overestimate potential tree cover;
thus, our full-potential forestation scenario (Bastin_Full) represents the upper bound
of global forestation potential. In this regard, we designed two additional scenarios
(Bastin_Refined_Climate and Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land) by progressively
introducing more realistic constraints to test the robustness of our results. These three
scenarios represent a range of possible forestation pathways, from the theoretical
maximum to the most practical feasible.
Bastin_Refined_Climate builds upon Bastin_Full by excluding regions with frequent
fires and where forestation would produce net warming due to reduced surface
albedo. This refinement addresses two major critiques of the Bastin et al.’s dataset:
overestimated potential in fire-prone grassland and savanna ecosystems, and the
neglect of forestation-caused regional warming due to reduced albedo65,66. Following
Fesenmyer et al.64, we used the 500 m MODIS Burned Area dataset to remove all non-
cropland areas experiencing two or more fires during 2002–2022, assuming that such
frequencies substantially limit tree density114. We further excluded regions where
albedo-induced radiative warming exceeds the cooling from carbon sequestration of
potential forestation, based on the dataset of Halser et al.115. These constraints
markedly reduce the estimated afforestation potential in tropical grassland and
savanna ecosystems, particularly across Africa (Supplementary Fig. 1b).
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land incorporated additional constraints on
Bastin_Refined_Climate by excluding croplands, built-up areas, and wetlands to
ensure land-use sustainability and feasibility. Urban and agricultural areas, given
their essential roles in food production and human livelihoods, were masked out using
the ESA CCI Global Land Cover dataset for 2000. Wetlands were excluded using the
Global Lakes and Wetlands Database (GLWD, version 2) to prevent potential losses
of large soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks following afforestation. Compared with the
Bastin_Refined_Climate scenario, the further reduction in forestation potential in
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land predominantly occurs in cropland-dominated regions
like Europe, African croplands, Southeast Asia, and eastern South America
(Supplementary Fig. 1c).” (Lines 627-657).
Both further constrained scenarios (Bastin_Refined_Climate and
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land) exhibit a latitudinal pattern of runoff responses
similar to that of the Bastin_Full scenario, with increases in the tropics and reductions
at high latitudes (Fig. R11). Using the Budyko framework to attribute forestation-
induced runoff changes, we find that the dominant role of forest-atmosphere
feedbacks in shaping the latitudinal gradient of runoff responses remains robust across
different afforestation scenarios (Fig. R12). While the overall pattern remains
consistent, discrepancies are present in regional responses among the scenarios. In
Bastin_Refined_Climate, reduced forestation area over tropical grasslands and
savannas leads to less strong tropical runoff increases. In
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land, the further exclusion of cropland and urban areas
weakens, but not reverses, the decrease runoff in some high-latitude regions. We have
incorporated the new results from these additional sensitivity tests into the revised
manuscript, as follows:
“Since the full-potential afforestation scenario using the Bastin et al.’s dataset may
overestimate the actual reforestation potential64–66, we further incorporated additional
constraints on the potential forestation maps to test the robustness of results. Building
on Bastin_Full, a new scenario (Bastin_Refined_Climate) additionally excludes areas

after afforestation, and another new scenario (Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land)
further excludes croplands, built-up lands, and wetlands. Our simulations forced by
refined potential forestation maps produced a latitudinal gradient of runoff responses
similar to that of Bastin_Full, though with regional difference in the hydrological
effects (Supplementary Fig. 5). Compared with Bastin_Full, reduced forestation area
over tropical grasslands and savannas leads to less strong tropical runoff increase;
and further exclusion of afforestation over croplands and urban areas in
Bastin_Refined_Climate&Land show less significant decreases in high-latitude
regions and weaker increases in low-latitude regions. (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 5).
In both afforestation scenarios, the contrasting pattern of enhanced tropical runoff
and suppressed high-latitude runoff remains evident.” (Lines 189-203);
“Furthermore, the two further constrained forestation scenarios consistently show
that forest-atmosphere feedbacks strongly shape the latitudinal gradient of runoff
responses (Supplementary Fig. 7).” (Lines 241-243).

(2) Reliability of simulated runoff
We conducted a validation of the simulated runoff against observed streamflow data
derived from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive (GSIM)11,12. In the
Supplementary Texts, we provide details on this streamflow database and describe the
data screening criteria and processing, as also copied here:
“We conducted a validation of the simulated runoff using streamflow observations
from the Global Streamflow Indices and Metadata Archive (GSIM)1,2, which provides
daily records of streamflow from over 30,000 stations worldwide. To ensure
comparability with model’s coarse spatial resolution and its lack of representation of
direct human interventions (e.g., dam construction, irrigation), we screened the
available catchments based the following criteria: (1) with a drainage area greater
than 20,000 km2; (2) with at least 15 years of complete annual streamflow records
between 1971 and 2010; (3) with ‘high’ or ‘medium’ boundary quality, indicating less
than 10% difference between the calculated and reported drainage area; (4) with
irrigation areas < 1% of total area or reservoir capacity < 10% of mean annual
streamflow; (5) Only catchments for which four homogeneity tests (i.e., the standard
normal homogeneity test3, the Buishand range test4, the Pettitt test5, and the von
Neumann ratio test6, adopted by the GSIM data) all fail to reject the null hypothesis of
no break-point in the time series at the 1% significance level were selected. The
catchmental irrigation area and reservoir capacity, and quality control for catchment
boundaries, are all derived from the GSIM metadata.
Applying these criteria led to a total of 270 catchments. The locations of these
catchments and the number of valid annual observations are shown in the
Supplementary Fig. 26a. For comparability with models’ runoff output, mean annual
runoff (in mm day-1) from observations were obtained by dividing the river discharge
(m3 day-1) by the station’s upstream catchment area (km2). For the simulated runoff by
IPSL and CESM (based on the CTL run), we first interpolated model output to a 1°
resolution. For each selected catchment, the catchment-scale runoff was calculated as
the areal-weighted average of grid cells falling within the catchment.”
(Supplementary Text 3).
Using streamflow observations from the 270 selected catchments (as shown in Fig.
R13a), we evaluated the performance of modelled runoff. As expected, IPSL-
simulated runoff exhibits notable deviations from observed values especially in large
catchments (Fig. R13b). This is because IPSL does not account for the effects of
urbanization, anthropogenic land-use changes, and river routing processes within the
catchments particularly those large ones. Despite this difference for specific
catchments, we find an overall significant positive correlation (r = 0.66, p < 0.01)
between the IPSL simulations and observations (Fig. 13b), indicating that IPSL
successfully captures characteristics of runoff in ‘wet’ versus ‘dry’ catchments.
Importantly, across all available catchments, the median difference between IPSL
estimates and observations is significantly indistinguishable from zero (Fig. 13d),
suggesting no systemic bias in IPSL simulations of runoff at the continental scale.
Furthermore, we find that IPSL outperforms CESM in runoff simulations. Evaluation
of CESM-based estimates show a weak, though significant, correlation (r) of 0.20 (p
< 0.01) (Fig. R13c), and a significant negative deviation of the modelled runoff from

The study primarily relies on IPSL-CM, with some additional analyses using CESM,
to simulate forestation effects. Dependence on one or two models raises concerns

resolution of IPSL-CM. Prior studies have demonstrated substantial inter-model
variability in forestation-induced changes in the water cycle: some models emphasize
moisture recycling, while others highlight atmospheric circulation adjustments. Even
within CMIP6 LUMIP experiments, large discrepancies exist among models under
comparable scenarios. I recommend integrating CESM results more prominently into
the main text and discussing model uncertainty in greater detail. It is difficult to place

[Response] We appreciate your valuable comment concerning the model dependency.
We understand your concern that relying on a single model may limit the robustness
of the conclusions, and this is indeed the motivation for us to include additional
simulations using CESM. The broadly consistent hydrological responses produced by
the two models, as well as our further verification with observation-based evidence
(see detailed response to your Major Comment 10), enhance our confidence in the
main findings. In our original manuscript, as you also note, we presented the CESM
results in the Supplementary Figures to complement the IPSL-CM results. In this
version, we retained this organization because our new evaluation against runoff
observations (see our response to your Major Comment 2) showed that IPSL notably
outperforms CESM in capturing the inter-catchment runoff variability the magnitudes
of observed runoff. Therefore, we prioritized IPSL-CM in the main text to better
represent the observationally constrained hydrological responses, while retaining
CESM results as complementary evidence of model robustness. Furthermore, while
CESM show broadly consistent results with IPSL, we detected nuanced regional
differences. In the revised manuscript, we have included a comparative discussion
about the IPSL and CESM results, highlighting the key differences between the two
structurally different models, written as: “Although CESM overall supports the IPSL-
based results, some regional discrepancies are notable due to structural and physical
differences between the two models. For example, in Southeast Asia, precipitation
increases exceed ET increases in IPSL, whereas the opposite pattern is simulated in
CESM (Fig.1 versus Supplementary Fig. 20). Our moisture budget decomposition
indicates that this difference stems from contrasting atmospheric circulation
responses: IPSL simulates an intensification of convective precipitation, while CESM
suggests a suppression (Supplementary Fig. 14c versus Supplementary Fig. 23c).”
(Lines 432-439).
In light of your comment, we have also compared our findings with previous model-
based assessments of global forestation impacts on the water cycle. While few studies
have explicitly examined runoff responses, several have analyzed precipitation
changes following idealized forestation28–31. All these model-based studies
consistently show a clear latitudinal gradient, with precipitation generally increasing
in the tropics and decreasing or showing weaker changes at higher latitudes. These
patterns are in line with our findings, despite regional discrepancies. For example, De
Hertog et al. (2024)31 and Portmann et al. (2022)28 report precipitation responses that
differ regionally from ours, which is unsurprising given their different experimental
designs (50% and 100% idealized afforestation, respectively) compared with our
climate-constrained potential afforestation scenario. Importantly, given that the
hydrological responses to afforestation and deforestation are generally opposite in
sign, the ‘deforest-globe’ scenario of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project
Phase 6 (CMIP6) Land Use Model Intercomparison Project (LUMIP) experiments —
provide multi-model evidence supporting our findings. For example, Ma et al. (2022)
highlighted the dominance of the atmospheric feedbacks induced by idealized global
deforestation, which exerted a similar latitudinal contrast in the response of runoff,
with reductions in the tropics and increases at mid-to-high latitudes. This
deforestation-driven pattern indirectly confirmed the latitudinal gradient of runoff
response identified in our study. We have incorporated these model-based discussions
into the revised manuscript, which now reads: “Our results are also corroborated by
previous model-based assessments of global forestation effects on the hydrological
cycle. For example, De Hertog et al.49 and Portmann et al.44 consistently show a clear
latitudinal gradient, with precipitation generally increasing in the tropics and
decreasing or showing weaker changes at higher latitudes, in line with our findings”
(Lines 212-216);
“The dominant role of forest-atmosphere feedbacks in shaping runoff responses is
further supported by an ensemble of idealized global deforestation simulations from
the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Land Use Model
Intercomparison Project (LUMIP), in which runoff responses exhibit a similar
latitudinal gradient of tropical reductions and mid-to-high latitude increases45. Given
that hydrological responses to afforestation and deforestation are generally opposite
in sign, this opposite pattern under deforestation indirectly corroborates the
robustness of our findings.” (Lines 439-446).
[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 4]
Lines 37–47: This section emphasizes carbon benefits, whereas the focus of this study
is on the hydrological cycle. Please consider rebalancing the discussion to align with
the core research objective.
The Budyko attribution approach is applied, yet the introduction lacks any description
or justification of this method.
Several statements in the introduction are not original contributions and should be
supported with appropriate citations.
The introduction discusses forestation-runoff relationships extensively but provides
limited context on latitudinal divergence, which is central to this study.
[Response] These are very useful comments that guide use to improve the focus and
clarity of our Introduction. Below we provide details about the revisions we made
according to each point. Collectively, these revisions enhance the clarity and
readability of the Introduction and reinforce its alignment with the study’s main
focus.
• Regarding the need to rebalance carbon and water: We agree that our original
version excessively emphasized on the carbon benefits of forestation. In the
revised Introduction, we have condensed this part and shifted the focus toward
hydrological impacts to better align with the core objective of this study, which
now read: “Forestation — including afforestation, reforestation and forest
management — has been advocated as a cost-effective nature-based strategy to
curb climate change by sequestering atmospheric CO (refs1–5). To optimize the
2
climate benefits of forestation, strategic tree planting in suitable locations is
essential. Previous studies indicate that, when moving from tropical to boreal
regions, not only does the carbon sequestration potential of forests decline, but
the biophysical effects also shift from cooling to warming mainly due to a
darkening of tree canopies, cautioning the limited climate benefits of afforestation
in boreal regions6–10.” (Lines 36-42).
• Regarding the Budyko framework: Following your suggestion, and to provide
readers with necessary methodological context, we have now added a brief
description and justification of the Budyko attribution approach, which now read:
“The runoff-suppressing effect of afforestation was also supported by analyses
based on the Budyko framework, which also offers an empirical approach for
attributing observed runoff changes into contributions from local atmospheric
changes (i.e., altered precipitation and potential evapotranspiration, PET) and
vegetation cover changes26,27” (Lines 62-66).
• Regarding the need for additional citations: We have carefully reviewed the
Introduction and added appropriate references to support several background
statements, ensuring that all non-original claims are now properly cited. For
example, we have included citations at the end of the sentence “In addition, these
simulations predominantly rely on idealized (e.g., 100% or 50%) or historical
afforestation/deforestation scenarios44,49,50” to acknowledge the relevant previous
modeling studies. Please refer to the new Introduction for all changes to citations.
• Regarding the discussion of latitudinal divergence: Following your advice, we
have clarified the scientific context and significance of our focus on the latitudinal
divergence in forestation-runoff relationships, which now reads: “Although the
influence of PET changes is often considered secondary to that of precipitation, it
can become more pronounced in energy-limited high-latitude regions45. This is
because the transition from snow-covered surfaces to darker forests substantially
increases surface net radiation10,51, which enhances PET and thus suppresses
runoff generation. Conversely, in tropical regions where the atmosphere is more
convectively unstable and oceanic moisture supply is abundant52–54, high rates of
moisture recycling over rainforests amplify precipitation responses to forest
expansion36,55. For example, previous modeling studies have suggested that large-
scale afforestation enhances precipitation more substantially in the tropics than in
boreal regions44,49. These coexisting and counteracting mechanisms imply the
balance between effects of precipitation and PET may vary geographically. So
far, it remains unknown about the net effect of forest-atmosphere feedbacks on
runoff, and the overall hydrological impact that further incorporates the direct
forest-driven ET increase.” (Lines 99-111).
[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 5]
The results section describes percentage changes, but some figures appear to display
absolute numerical changes. Please clarify this inconsistency.
[Response] We appreciate this useful comment. In our analyses based on the water-
balance and Budyko attribution frameworks, we used absolute numerical changes to
retain the physical meaning and comparability among different water‐balance
components (e.g., to assess the rate of runoff change relative to precipitation).
In contrast, in the Results section, we expressed the results as percentage changes when
comparing the hydrological responses between cold and warm regions. This is
because the magnitude of mean runoff differs substantially between these regions
(with generally larger runoff in warm areas). Using relative changes allows for a more
meaningful comparison of forest–atmosphere feedbacks across the two climate zones.
We have clarified this inconsistency in the revised manuscript to avoid confusion and
enhance readability, written as: “Given that mean runoff differs by several-fold
between warm and cold regions, we used relative rather than absolute changes in our
subsequent analysis to facilitate comparison of forestation-induced hydrological
responses.” (Lines 267-269).
[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 6]
Figure 1 reveals several unexpected findings that warrant more careful discussion. For
example, precipitation changes exceed evapotranspiration changes in magnitude. This
suggests that large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts and cascading moisture
recycling effects may play a substantial role. In Southeast Asia, minor changes in
evapotranspiration appear to trigger pronounced precipitation increases. However,
these phenomena are not reproduced by CESM, highlighting the model dependence of
the results. Supplementary Figure 4 statistics should be incorporated into the main
text to strengthen the argument. Does CESM support the key findings of IPSL-CM
simulations? The results for warm regions appear to differ considerably. The results
for China in Figure 1d and Supplementary Figure 4d seem inconsistent with prior
studies. Have the authors compared their findings with recent global forestation-water
cycle simulations? There appear to be notable discrepancies.

King JA, Weber J, Lawrence P, Roe S, Swann ALS, Val Martin M. Global and

[Response] Thank you very much for your careful review and for these insightful
detailed comments regarding the robustness of our model-based results. We see you
raised several important points concerning (1) the larger precipitation response
compared to evapotranspiration (ET), (2) the comparison between IPSL-CM and
CESM, and (3) consistency with previous studies. Our detailed responses to each of
them are provided below.
(1) On the larger precipitation increase relative to evapotranspiration
Yes, our model simulations suggests that precipitation increases more strongly than
ET, and this is a robust signal as both trends are statistically significant. This indicates
that global forestation alters precipitation not only through direct or cascading
recycling of evaporated water from new forests, but also by modifying large-scale
atmospheric circulation and boosting atmospheric moisture convergence. Our analysis
indicate that forestation-driven circulation changes enhance both horizontal and
vertical moisture transport in tropical monsoon regions (Fig. R14), allowing more
oceanic moisture to be advected inland. Thus, in monsoon regions where precipitation
primarily originates from oceanic sources, forestation strengthens the transport of
moisture from the ocean to land. This is supported by previous studies showing that
vegetation changes in monsoon regions can affect rainfall by perturbing sea-breeze
circulations32–38. We further compared our results with studies that quantified the
recycling of new forests-sourced moisture (ET) using moisture-tracking models.
Those studies, without accounting for atmospheric moisture convergence, suggest that
ET increases exceed precipitation increases39,40. This finding, when compared with
our fully coupled simulations, revealed the essential role of atmospheric moisture
convergence, in determining the balance between precipitation and ET changes. We
have discussed the role of large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts in the
hydrological response to afforestation in in Lines 486–498 of the revised manuscript.

(2) On the comparison between IPSL-CM and CESM
To evaluate whether CESM supports the key findings of IPSL-CM, we also applied
the Budyko framework to decompose the CESM-simulated runoff changes into the
contributions of atmospheric feedbacks and land surface changes (Fig. R15). The
CESM results also indicate that forest-atmosphere feedbacks primarily shape the
spatial pattern of runoff responses to forestation. To understand the role of forest-
atmosphere feedbacks, we further performed the water vapor budget analysis for
precipitation changes and the attribution of PET changes using net radiation and
atmospheric moisture demand. This additional analysis confirms that CESM supports
the main results from IPSL (Fig. R16). For instance, CESM also suggests that the
pronounced precipitation increases in tropical regions primarily arise from enhanced
horizontal and vertical moisture transport associated with circulation changes.
While CESM overall supports the main conclusions derived from IPSL, some
regional discrepancies are expected given the structural and physical differences
between the two models. For example, in Southeast Asia (as you mentioned),
precipitation increases exceed ET increases in IPSL, whereas the opposite occurs in
CESM. Our moisture budget decomposition indicates that this difference stems from
contrasting atmospheric circulation responses: IPSL simulates stronger convective
precipitation, while CESM shows a reduction in convective rainfall (comparing Fig.
R14 and Fig. R17). We chose not to include CESM results in the main text because
CESM exhibits lower reliability in reproducing observed runoff variations (see our
response to Comment 2). However, in line with the reviewer’s suggestion, we now
provide a more detailed discussion of the differences between IPSL and CESM in the
revised manuscript, which now read:
“To assess the robustness of our model-based findings, we also performed equilibrium
experiments using an independent model, Community Earth System Model (CESM).
This model reproduces a similar latitudinal (thermal) pattern of forestation-induced
runoff changes, with increases in warm regions and decreases in cold regions, albeit
with slightly different magnitudes (Supplementary Fig. 20). Consistent with IPSL-CM,
CESM indicates that forest-atmosphere feedbacks predominantly shape the latitudinal
gradient of runoff responses (Supplementary Fig. 21). Furthermore, both the water
vapor budget analysis for precipitation changes and the attribution of PET changes
using net radiation and atmospheric moisture demand corroborate the main
conclusions derived from IPSL-CM (Supplementary Fig. 22). For instance, regarding
precipitation responses to afforestation, CESM confirms that the pronounced
increases in warm regions primarily result from enhanced horizontal and vertical
moisture transport driven by circulation adjustments (Supplementary Fig. 22d).
Although CESM overall supports the IPSL-based results, some regional discrepancies
are notable due to structural and physical differences between the two models. For
example, in Southeast Asia, precipitation increases exceed ET increases in IPSL,
whereas the opposite pattern is simulated in CESM (Fig.1 versus Supplementary Fig.
20). Our moisture budget decomposition indicates that this difference stems from
contrasting atmospheric circulation responses: IPSL simulates an intensification of
convective precipitation, while CESM suggests a suppression (Supplementary Fig.
14c versus Supplementary Fig. 23c).” (Lines 421-439).

(3) On the comparison with previous studies
We also compared our findings with previous global and regional afforestation-
hydrology simulations. Caution is needed for interpreting discrepancies across studies
as they may arise from different experimental design and temporal focus. Our
experimental setup represents equilibrium-state responses to idealized 100%
afforestation28,30,31 constrained by present-day climate, whereas many previous studies
examined transient or historical reforestation trajectories41. For instance, Li et al.41
examined transient hydrological responses to observed afforestation in China, while
King et al.29 explored transient climate feedbacks of afforestation under SSP1-2.6.
Such differences in timescale and forcing can introduce difference to the simulated
patterns.
Your observation that both IPSL and CESM show larger increases in water yield over
China compared to Li et al.41 can be explained by differences in spatial aggregation.
Li et al. (2023) reported near-zero national mean change because opposing local
effects—precipitation increases in southeastern China and decreases in northern
regions—offset each other. When examined regionally, their results also show that
precipitation increases exceed ET increases in the humid southeast, which aligns
closely with our findings. Moreover, our conclusions are further supported by
multiple independent model lines of evidence. Other idealized GCM experiments28,31,
and high-resolution regional climate simulations35, consistently indicate increased P–
ET over China, further supporting our conclusions. In the revised manuscript, we
have discussed our results with several other modeling studies to reinforce the
robustness of our conclusions, as detailed below:
“Our results are also corroborated by previous model-based assessments of global
forestation effects on the hydrological cycle. For example, De Hertog et al.49 and
Portmann et al.44 consistently show a clear latitudinal gradient, with precipitation
generally increasing in the tropics and decreasing or showing weaker changes at
higher latitudes, in line with our findings” (Lines 212-216);
“The dominant role of forest-atmosphere feedbacks in shaping runoff responses is
further supported by an ensemble of idealized global deforestation simulations from
the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Land Use Model
Intercomparison Project (LUMIP), in which runoff responses exhibit a similar
latitudinal gradient of tropical reductions and mid-to-high latitude increases45. Given
that hydrological responses to afforestation and deforestation are generally opposite
in sign, this opposite pattern under deforestation indirectly corroborates the
robustness of our findings.” (Lines 439-446).
“For example, previous modeling studies based on a regional climate model (40-km
resolution)90 or a zoomed IPSL-CM have suggested enhanced runoff in response to
historical afforestation in China40, consistent with our GCM-based results.” (Lines
528-531).

[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 8]
Additionally, how have the authors accounted for internal climate variability in the
Budyko attribution?
[Response] Thank you for this valuable comment. We appreciate this opportunity to
clarify how internal climate variability was accounted for in our attribution. In the
Budyko framework, there is an assumption of steady state of the catchments’ water
balance. Our equilibrium simulation perfectly meets this assumption, though there is
still strong internal climate variability in the time series. In our original analysis, we
took the average of the last 30 years of the 100-year simulation, expected to also
average out the internal climate variability.
With your comment, we recognized that the 30-year averaging window, while
effective for averaging out interannual to inter-decadal variability, may not eliminate
the influence of multi-decadal oscillations. To further control for potential influence
of multi-decadal climate variability, and considering that the simulations reached an
equilibrium after about 40 years, now in the revised manuscript, we analyze the last
60 years of the equilibrium period. The new results remain consistent with our
original finding of contrasting forestation-driven runoff changes in tropical versus
high-latitude regions (see new figures in the revised manuscript). This indicates that
our main results are robust to the additional exclusion of multi-decadal oscillations.
We have explained the reason for selecting the final 60 years of data in the revised
Methods section, as follows: “selecting 60 years also helps reduce the potential
influence of inter-decadal and multi-decadal climate variability” (Lines 574-575).
Furthermore, to more comprehensively assess the potential effects of climate
variability across different timescales, we implemented a bootstrap resampling
approach using data from the last 60 years of the equilibrium period. Specifically, we
performed 1,000 random resamplings (with replacement) of 30-, 40-, 50-, and 60-year
subsets, each time decomposing runoff changes into the atmospheric feedback and
land surface components based on the Budyko framework. The bootstrap ensemble
means derived from 30-, 40-, 50-, and 60-year subsets all yield consistent results (Fig.
R22), demonstrating that internal climate variability has minimal impact on our
primary findings. This methodology is now detailed in the revised Methods, and the
associated results have been incorporated into the new version, which reads:
“In addition to the use of 60-year equilibrium simulations, we further examined how
climate variability across different timescales might affect the attribution of runoff
responses. To this end, we implemented a bootstrap resampling approach to generate
1,000 random year samples (with replacement from the final 60 years), for 30-, 40-,
50-, and 60-year timescales, respectively. For each sample, the forestation-induced
runoff change was calculated as the difference between the SCE and CTL simulations
and further decomposed into atmospheric feedback and land-surface components
using the Budyko framework. The mean of the 1,000 realizations represents the
average runoff response for each timescale. The ensemble means derived from the
30-, 40-, 50-, and 60-year subsets produced results consistent with our main findings
(Supplementary Fig. 9), indicating that internal climate variability has minimal
influence on our conclusions.” (Lines 768-778 in Methods);
“In addition, we assessed how inter-decadal to multi-decadal climate variability
influence the attribution results by varying time windows of the equilibrium
simulations based on a bootstrap approach (Methods). The latitudinal pattern of
runoff responses and the leading role of forest-atmosphere feedbacks are consistent
across all time windows, indicating negligible influence of internal climate variability
on our results (Supplementary Fig. 9).” (Lines 253-258 in Results).

[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 9]
The Budyko attribution approach primarily considers first-order controls (mean
climate and land surface characteristics) on runoff. Yet, forestation-induced changes in
precipitation characteristics (e.g., rainfall intensity, fraction of precipitation as snow)
may substantially alter runoff generation processes and soil moisture availability for
evapotranspiration.
[Response] We very much appreciate this constructive feedback, which motivated us
to reconsider the influence of precipitation characteristics on runoff generation within
the Budyko attribution framework. As you kindly pointed out, the Budyko framework
primarily accounts for mean climatic conditions (precipitation and PET) and land
surface characteristics, and in the data-based approximation of n, the effects of
precipitation characteristics (e.g., rainfall intensity, fraction of snowfall) are implicitly
incorporated into this land surface term. This limitation, which is well recognized
within the ecohydrology community, may bias our interpretation of n changes as
solely resulting from land surface processes in our attribution of forestation-induced
runoff changes.
To address potential bias related to precipitation characteristics, we separated
precipitation and runoff changes due to altered precipitation characteristics and
incorporated these into effects of atmospheric changes, following the approach
proposed by Zhou et al.25. We further decomposed the effects of the atmospheric
feedbacks (due to altered mean precipitation, PET, and precipitation characteristics),
and land surface changes (only due to catchment properties) on runoff under the
modified Budyko framework. In particular, this modification ensures applicability in
cold regions because snow-related biases have been corrected. The results based on
this extended method are consistent with our main conclusions, showing that forest-
atmosphere feedbacks primarily drive the latitudinal contrast in afforestation-induced
runoff changes, with decreases at high latitudes and increases in the tropics (Fig.
R23). In the revised MS, we have added a detailed description of this Budyko
attribution method with correction to effects of precipitation characteristics and of

[Reviewer #2 Major Comment 10]
Finally, can the authors provide observational evidence to support their model-based
findings? Robustness checks relying solely on model-derived data are less persuasive;
validation against independent observations is critical to establish confidence.
[Response] We appreciate this useful comment which motivated us to validate our
model-based results against independent observations. We agree that observational
evidence can strengthen confidence in our modeled responses. However, this
validation is precluded by the unavailable, or unreliable, observations of vegetation
feedbacks on the climate system. The signal of climate feedbacks is often intertwined
with vegetation responses to climate. Many observation-based studies instead used the
space-for-time substitution to quantify potential climate feedbacks of land cover
changes, assuming that forested and non-forested landscapes share similar
atmospheric backgrounds. This assumption neglects the influence of forest change on
atmospheric circulation, causing remote hydrological responses by redistributing
moisture and changing precipitation patterns. Given such limitations of conventional
observation-based methods, there is no ground truth for validating our modelled
hydrological feedbacks.
Nonetheless, for regions where precipitation sources largely from local ET (i.e., with
strong local moisture recycling), the signature of forest-atmosphere feedbacks might
be detectable in observational data. To explore this possibility, we analyzed the spatial
sensitivity of surface moisture balance (P minus ET) to tree cover. In this analysis, we
employed precipitation from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation
(MSWEP, an integration of gauge, satellite, and model data) dataset (1°×1°
resolution), ET from the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM)
dataset, and forest cover maps from the European Space Agency Climate Change
Initiative (ESA CCI) 300 m land cover dataset. Specifically, for each 1° × 1°
vegetated grid cell, we performed spatial moving-window (3×3) regressions of
precipitation (or ET) against forest cover, near-surface air temperature (from Climatic
Research Unit, CRU), and incoming shortwave radiation (from Clouds and the Earth’s
Radiant Energy System, CERES) to estimate the precipitation (or ET) sensitivity to
forest cover fraction. The difference between precipitation and ET sensitivities
represents the sensitivity of P–ET to forest cover change, which approximates runoff
over long-term timescales. We then selected pixels where both precipitation and ET
sensitivities to forest change were statistically significant (p < 0.05).
Fig. R24 (also appears as Supplementary Fig. 6 in the revised version) Observation-
estimated sensitivity of precipitation minus evapotranspiration (P–ET) to forest cover
changes. The values are binned according to latitude: high latitudes (>60°), mid-

(horizontal lines), 25th, 75th quartiles, maximum and minimum values (top
and bottom of the whiskers) and outliers (dots) of P–ET sensitivity. The number displayed
above each bin indicates the total count of grid cells in which both the local

This observation-based analysis shows a clear latitudinal contrast: P–ET overall
decreases with forest cover gain in most high-latitude regions but increases in the
tropics (Fig. R24), consistent with our model-based findings. There are a considerable
fraction of grids showing opposing signs, which is likely because this empirical
approach cannot fully remove the moisture redistribution effects of circulation.
Moreover, Ma et al.26 similarly estimated the sensitivity of P–ET to forest cover
changes by directly regressing P–ET against forest cover using observations. Their
results showed that historical deforestation mainly decreased P–ET in the tropics
while increasing it in high-latitude regions. Although the hydrological responses to
deforestation and afforestation are asymmetric in magnitude, they generally present
opposite signs. Therefore, the results of Ma et al.26 provide additional support for the
robustness of our findings. We have included this observational verification in the
Methods and discussed its support for our model-based conclusions in the main text.
The added texts read as follows:
“Observed sensitivity of P–ET to forest cover changes
To quantify the observation-based sensitivity of P–ET to forest cover change, we used
precipitation data from the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP;
1° × 1° resolution), ET data from the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model

Research Unit Time-Series (CRU TS; 0.5° × 0.5°), and incoming shortwave radiation
from the Clouds and the Earth’s Radiant Energy System (CERES; 1° × 1°).

atmospheric moisture, which can obscure the forest-precipitation signal, we analyzed
20-year means (2001–2020) rather than individual years. All datasets were resampled
to a common 1° × 1° grid to match the coarser spatial resolution of model outputs.

against forest cover, air temperature, and incoming shortwave radiation within a 3 ×
3 window centred on the pixel, to estimate the sensitivity of precipitation (or ET) to
forest cover change. The difference between precipitation and ET sensitivities
represents the sensitivity of P–ET to forest cover changes, which approximates runoff
responses over long-term scales. It is important to note that most observation-based
space-for-time substitution approaches assume that forested and non-forested
landscapes share similar atmospheric backgrounds, and thus cannot capture the
influence of forest change on atmospheric circulation that redistributes moisture and
affects precipitation. We hypothesize that this moisture redistribution effects of
circulation diminishes the local forest–precipitation signal. Hence, we only selected

“To further verify our simulated latitudinal gradient of runoff responses to forestation,
we calculated the observed sensitivity of precipitation minus ET (P–ET) to forest

[Response] Thank you for this insightful comment, which prompted us to examine
the individual components of ET in our afforestation experiments. In our analysis,
modelled ET changes were decomposed into the four processes: transpiration, canopy
interception, soil evaporation, and sublimation (Fig. R25). Our results show that
forestation-induced ET increases primarily result from enhanced canopy transpiration
and interception, though partly offset by a simultaneous reduction in soil evaporation.
This reduction occurs because the expanded canopy cover shades the soil surface,
reducing available energy for evaporation, and decreases near-surface vapor pressure
deficit that drives soil evaporation44. In addition, afforestation leads to a slight but
significant increase in sublimation at mid-to-high latitudes in the Northern
Hemisphere, likely due to enhanced snow interception by the expanded forest canopy.
